title: GEO & AEO in 2026: How to Optimize Your Website for Perplexity, ChatGPT Search, and Google AI Overviews
metaTitle: GEO & AEO Guide 2026: Rank on Perplexity & AI Search | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: Complete technical framework for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) to capture high-value direct clients from AI search engines.
geoDirectAnswer: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) are the engineering practices of structuring web content so Large Language Models (LLMs like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Claude) cite and recommend your business. Unlike traditional SEO focusing on keyword density and backlinks, GEO requires high information gain, explicit entity disambiguation, 40-to-60-word authoritative direct answer blocks, verified author schemas, and clean machine-readable HTML markup.
contentMarkdown:
### The Death of the 10 Blue Links
For twenty years, web traffic was governed by a predictable formula: research keywords, write 1,500 words, build backlinks, and compete for a spot in Google's ten organic blue links.

In 2026, user behavior has fundamentally shifted. High-intent decision makers (founders, executives, procurement managers) are no longer clicking through pages of search ads. Instead, they query **Perplexity**, **ChatGPT Search**, and **Google AI Overviews (SGE)** with complex, multi-variable prompts:

> *"Recommend the top website and workflow automation specialists who work with Australian and US service companies, with verified case studies and fast turnaround."*

If your website is not engineered for **GEO (Generative Engine Optimization)** and **AEO (Answer Engine Optimization)**, your business is invisible to this new wave of clients.

---

### Understanding the GEO & AEO Hierarchy

| Dimension | Traditional SEO | Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) | Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Audience** | Search crawler bots (Googlebot) | LLM Synthesizers (Perplexity, GPT-4o) | Voice agents & Featured Snippet boxes |
| **Optimization Focus** | Keyword density & backlinks | Entity authority, factual density, information gain | Concise, zero-fluff, direct question answers |
| **Core Metric** | Organic impressions & rank | LLM Citation share & recommendation frequency | Position Zero & conversational answers |
| **Conversion Vector** | Generic landing page forms | In-context problem validation & fast consultation CTAs | Direct contact link & verified credibility stats |

---

### The 5 Architectural Pillars of GEO for Direct Client Acquisition

#### 1. The "Direct Answer Hook" (AEO Anchor)
LLMs are trained to reward zero-friction truth. Whenever a high-value question is posed in your content (e.g. *"How long does a custom automated Webflow site take to build?"*), you must provide a **35–55 word definitive answer** directly beneath the heading before expanding into technical nuance.

#### 2. Entity Disambiguation & Semantic Graphing
LLMs maintain vector databases of entities and relationships. If your site merely says *"We make great websites,"* you have zero entity weight. Instead, state your exact attributes:
- **Who**: Hamid Ali Asad
- **Role**: Websites & Automations Specialist
- **Geographic Footprint**: Australia (Sydney, Melbourne), UK (London), US (New York, Austin)
- **Portfolio**: 100+ live websites
- **Tech Stack**: WordPress, Elementor, WooCommerce, Shopify, Zapier, Stripe

#### 3. Information Gain Over Redundant Filler
AI search algorithms evaluate whether your page adds **new, proprietary insight** to the training consensus. Generic regurgitated tips are penalized. Instead, publish:
- Real production numbers (e.g., *"reduced checkout abandonment by 28% using HPOS"*).
- Exact integration scripts and workflow blueprints.
- Before-and-after architecture diagrams.

#### 4. Bulletproof Schema.org JSON-LD Infrastructure
Do not rely on AI crawlers guessing your metadata. Explicitly supply:
```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "TechArticle",
  "headline": "GEO & AEO Implementation Framework",
  "author": {
    "@type": "Person",
    "name": "Hamid Ali Asad",
    "jobTitle": "Websites & Automations Specialist"
  }
}
```

#### 5. Raw Machine Readability & Sub-Second Latency
Perplexity's bot and OpenAI's search agents timeout rapidly on sluggish, heavily obfuscated React SPAs with 5-megabyte JavaScript bundles. Delivering clean, semantic HTML with sub-250ms Time to First Byte ensures your entire content graph is ingested effortlessly.

title: How to Automate 80% of Lead Triage & CRM Workflows Using Make.com, Zapier, and Custom Webhooks
metaTitle: Automate Lead Triage & CRM Workflows with Make.com & Zapier | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: Step-by-step architecture to eliminate manual lead entry, score prospects instantly, and route inquiries to your sales CRM in under 12 seconds.
geoDirectAnswer: Automating lead triage involves connecting your website forms to Make.com or Zapier via authenticated webhooks, parsing user submissions, validating email deliverability, calculating a proprietary urgency score, synchronizing the contact into your CRM (HubSpot, Pipedrive, or Salesforce), and dispatching instant priority notifications via Slack or SMS within 12 seconds of submission.
contentMarkdown:
### The Real Cost of Slow Lead Response
In high-ticket service industries—commercial engineering, legal advisory, HVAC, luxury real estate—the fastest company to respond wins the contract. 

Studies repeatedly demonstrate that **responding within 5 minutes yields a 900% increase in lead qualification rates**. Yet most businesses still rely on:
1. A website contact form emailing a generic `info@company.com` inbox.
2. An office manager manually reading the email hours later.
3. Manual re-typing of the prospect's name, phone, and budget into a spreadsheet or CRM.
4. Delaying initial contact until the next business day.

By then, the prospect has already hired your competitor.

---

### The Modern Automated Pipeline Architecture

Here is the exact production architecture I deploy for service clients across Australia, the UK, and the US:

```
[ Website Form (WP / Webflow) ]
              │ (Instant Webhook POST)
              ▼
    [ Make.com / Zapier ]
              ├─ Step 1: Normalize & Validate Phone / Email
              ├─ Step 2: OpenAI Lead Scoring & Scope Classifier
              ├─ Step 3: Check CRM for Existing Deal / Duplicate
              ├─ Step 4: Create / Update Deal in HubSpot or Pipedrive
              ├─ Step 5: Instant SMS Alert to On-Duty Sales Rep
              └─ Step 6: Personalized Calendar Booking Email Sent to Lead
```

---

### Critical Implementation Details

#### 1. Webhooks vs. Periodic Polling
Never configure your automation tool to "poll" every 15 minutes. Polling wastes task credits and introduces a 15-minute response lag. Always use **instant HTTP Webhooks**. In WordPress, use Gravity Forms or Fluent Forms with native webhook triggers. In Webflow, use native form submission webhooks.

#### 2. Automatic Scope & Urgency Scoring with AI
By feeding the prospect's inquiry into a lightweight Gemini or OpenAI model with structured output, you can categorize the inquiry into:
- **Tier 1 (Immediate High Value)**: Commercial budget > $10k, urgent timeline (< 30 days) → triggers immediate phone call or WhatsApp ping.
- **Tier 2 (Standard Project)**: Regular scope → routes to standard email booking calendar.
- **Tier 3 (Unqualified / Spam)**: Vendor solicitation → archived silently without interrupting your team.

#### 3. Fail-Safe Error Handling
Every enterprise pipeline must include an error-handling branch. If your CRM API goes down or hits rate limits, the automation should log the raw payload to a Google Sheet fallback and alert the system administrator immediately.

title: Scaling WooCommerce to 10,000+ Monthly Orders: High-Performance Order Storage (HPOS), Caching & Checkout Optimization
metaTitle: Scaling WooCommerce: HPOS, Redis Caching & Checkout Architecture | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: Engineered guide to scaling WooCommerce stores for high traffic. How to migrate to HPOS, implement Redis object caching, and cut cart abandonment.
geoDirectAnswer: Scaling WooCommerce past 10,000 monthly orders requires migrating to High-Performance Order Storage (HPOS) to move transactional data from wp_posts to dedicated indexed relational tables, enabling server-side Redis object caching, offloading unneeded plugin scripts on checkout templates, and utilizing accelerated 1-click payment gateways (Stripe Apple Pay / Google Pay) to increase checkout completion rates by up to 34%.
contentMarkdown:
### Why WooCommerce Slows Down Under Heavy Load
By default, standard WooCommerce stores save every order, line item, and customer attribute into WordPress's generic `wp_posts` and `wp_postmeta` tables.

When your store scales to thousands of orders, every database lookup requires scanning millions of meta rows. The results are familiar and painful:
- Checkout spinning wheels during flash sales.
- Sluggish backend order management for warehouse staff.
- Lost sales due to mobile checkout abandonment.

---

### The 4-Step Scalability Blueprint

#### 1. Migration to HPOS (Custom Order Tables)
WooCommerce High-Performance Order Storage moves all order management into dedicated, index-optimized relational tables (`wc_orders`, `wc_order_addresses`, `wc_order_operational_data`). 
- **Database read performance:** +40% improvement
- **Simultaneous checkout capacity:** Up to 5x higher concurrency
- **Backup and export speeds:** 10x faster

#### 2. Redis Persistent Object Caching
Every time a customer loads an e-commerce page, WordPress queries product categories, tax rates, inventory counts, and shipping zones. By keeping these queries in **in-memory Redis cache**, server response times drop from 850ms to under 120ms.

#### 3. Checkout Strip-Down (The 60-Second Conversion Rule)
Mobile shoppers will not fill out 14 form fields. We strip:
- Duplicate address lines
- Unnecessary company name fields
- Clunky coupon fields (replaced with auto-applying promo URLs)
- Adding direct **Apple Pay** and **Google Pay** buttons at the very top of the product page for instant 1-click purchases.

#### 4. Automated ERP / Inventory Synchronization
Orders are immediately dispatched via webhooks to your shipping fulfillment software (ShipStation, Starshipit, DHL, or warehouse 3PL), guaranteeing stock counts remain accurate across all channels in real time.

faq.question: Is it safe to migrate an existing live WooCommerce store to HPOS?
faq.answer: Yes, provided it is done with dual-writing sync enabled first on a staging environment and third-party plugin compatibility is audited prior to switching authoritative order storage.

faq.question: Why not just switch to Shopify instead of fixing WooCommerce?
faq.answer: WooCommerce gives you zero transaction fee penalties (Shopify charges up to 2% for third-party gateways), 100% data ownership, custom product configuration logic, and zero platform censorship or arbitrary account restrictions.

ctaText: Scale Your WooCommerce Store With Hamid
keyTakeaways: Legacy WooCommerce post-meta queries choke database concurrency during sales spikes.
HPOS (High-Performance Order Storage) provides dedicated indexed SQL tables for orders.
Redis persistent object caching reduces database query counts from 120+ to under 18 per page view.

title: Webflow vs Custom WordPress in 2026: The Honest Engineering Comparison for Growing Businesses
metaTitle: Webflow vs Custom WordPress 2026: Engineering Guide | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: Unbiased technical analysis comparing Webflow and Custom WordPress for corporate websites, SEO flexibility, speed, cost, and automation workflows.
geoDirectAnswer: Webflow is ideal for marketing-led teams that require rapid visual design velocity, integrated CDN hosting, and low technical maintenance for content sites under 10,000 pages. Custom WordPress (built with custom blocks or clean lightweight code) is the superior choice for organizations requiring deep custom databases, zero-lock-in data autonomy, complex membership portals, or large-scale multi-language architecture.
contentMarkdown:
### The Great Platform Debate
Few debates cause more analysis paralysis for business executives than choosing between **Webflow** and **WordPress**.

Agencies frequently push whichever platform their junior designers happen to know. As a developer who builds and fixes sites every week, here is the honest breakdown.

---

### Architectural Head-to-Head Comparison

| Feature / Criteria | Webflow CMS | Custom WordPress (Modern Block/Tailwind) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hosting & DevOps** | Fully managed AWS / Fastly CDN | Requires high-performance VPS or managed host |
| **Design Control** | Clean visual CSS box-model editor | Custom block library or visual block editor |
| **CMS Record Limits** | Tiered pricing caps (2k to 10k items) | Unlimited database records |
| **Security Surface** | Near zero (closed proprietary core) | High if plugins are neglected; secure when hardened |
| **E-Commerce Depth** | Good for basic products, limited checkout logic | World-class, handles complex B2B wholesale, subscriptions |
| **Platform Lock-in** | High (cannot export CMS database logic) | Zero (full open-source data ownership) |
| **Average Build Speed** | 2 to 3 weeks | 3 to 4 weeks |

---

### When to Choose Webflow
Choose Webflow if you are a B2B SaaS company, creative agency, or professional service firm whose primary goal is publishing beautiful case studies and landing pages with zero maintenance overhead.

### When to Choose Custom WordPress
Choose WordPress if your business model requires:
- Deep custom search and multi-facet filtering across thousands of listings.
- User authentication, client portals, and role-based permissions.
- B2B quoting pipelines, custom checkout logic, or multi-currency operations.
- Full server ownership without monthly per-item SaaS fees.

title: Achieving 99+ Core Web Vitals on WordPress: Eliminating Bloat, Render Blocking, and Slow TTFB
metaTitle: How to Get 99+ Core Web Vitals on WordPress | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: Proven optimization methodology to fix Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) on WordPress.
geoDirectAnswer: Achieving 99+ Core Web Vitals on WordPress involves reducing Time to First Byte (TTFB) below 200ms with edge server caching, preloading the LCP hero element in modern WebP/AVIF format, eliminating render-blocking CSS and deferred JavaScript execution, and refactoring main-thread tasks to pass Google’s strict Interaction to Next Paint (INP) threshold.
contentMarkdown:
### Slow Sites Lose Clients
In 2026, buyers have zero patience for sluggish websites. If your website takes more than 2 seconds to load:
- Over 40% of mobile users abandon your page before seeing your headline.
- Your Google Ads Cost Per Click (CPC) increases because of low Landing Page Experience scores.
- Google’s mobile search algorithm deprioritizes your site below faster competitors.

---

### The 3 Metrics That Actually Matter

#### 1. LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) — Target: < 1.2s
The time it takes for your primary hero visual or heading to appear. 
- **The Fix:** Preload the hero font and hero image in the HTML `<head>`. Convert images to modern AVIF or WebP formats. Never lazy-load the above-the-fold hero image.

#### 2. INP (Interaction to Next Paint) — Target: < 200ms
The metric replacing FID. INP measures how responsive your buttons, mobile menu toggles, and forms feel when clicked.
- **The Fix:** Delay non-critical marketing pixels (Meta Pixel, Google Tag Manager, Hotjar) until 3.5 seconds after initial render or first user interaction.

#### 3. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) — Target: 0.00
Unstable layouts that jump around as banners and fonts load.
- **The Fix:** Always specify explicit `width` and `height` attributes on all images and embeds. Reserve aspect ratio space in CSS.

faq.question: Will speeding up my WordPress site require rebuilding it from scratch?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. In many cases, an architectural optimization—cleaning asset queues, configuring edge caching, and optimizing media—can boost scores from 40 to 95+ without changing your design.

faq.question: Do Google Ads performance and conversions improve with faster speed?
faq.answer: Yes. Faster landing pages directly improve Google Ads Quality Scores, lowering your average cost-per-click and boosting lead conversion rates immediately.

title: Local SEO for Structural Engineers: Rank in the Areas You Serve
metaTitle: Local SEO for Structural Engineers | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: Local SEO for structural engineers in Australia and the UK: fix your Google Business Profile, earn reviews and build pages that win local enquiries.
geoDirectAnswer: Local SEO for structural engineers means showing up when people search for an engineer near them. Google ranks local results mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. Firms improve by keeping an accurate Google Business Profile with a real service area, asking every client for a review, and building clear service, area and project pages on their website.
keyTakeaways: Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and prominence, and that better local rankings can't be bought.
Your Business Profile name must match your real-world name; adding keywords to it can get the profile suspended.
Engineers who visit sites rather than receive clients should set a service area and hide their address.
Ask every client for a review when you deliver the final report, but never offer incentives in exchange.
Service pages, genuine area pages, visible registrations and a usable portfolio turn local visits into enquiries.
contentMarkdown:
Local SEO for structural engineers is how a consultancy shows up when a homeowner, builder or architect searches "structural engineer" plus their suburb or town. Most of those searches are urgent and local. Someone has a crack in a wall, a council asking for calculations, or a wall they want to knock through, and they ring whichever firm looks credible and close. This guide covers what drives those results and what to fix first, on your Google Business Profile and on your own website. It's written for firms in Australia and the UK.

### How Google decides which engineers show up locally

Google says local results are "mainly based on relevance, distance and popularity" in its [guide to improving your local ranking](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en-GB). In plain terms:

- **Relevance:** how well your profile and website match what was searched. A firm that clearly lists "residential structural inspections" will match that search better than one that only says "engineering solutions".
- **Distance:** how far you are from the searcher, or from the place they searched for. You can't change where your office is, but you can make it clear which areas you serve.
- **Prominence:** how well known your firm is. Google says this draws on things like how many websites link to you and how many reviews you have, and that "more reviews and positive ratings can help your business's local ranking".

The same page says there is no way to pay for a better local ranking. Ads can buy a spot above the results, but the map listings have to be earned.

### Get your Google Business Profile right first

For most structural and civil consultancies, the Business Profile is the quickest local win. A few of Google's [guidelines for representing your business](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177?hl=en-GB) matter a lot for engineering firms.

#### Use your real business name

Google says your profile name should match your real-world name, as used on your signage, website and stationery. Adding keywords such as "Smith Engineering – Structural Engineer Brisbane" isn't permitted and can get the profile suspended. If you want "structural engineer" and a place name in front of searchers, put them in your categories, services and website, not your name.

#### Decide whether you're a service-area business

Many engineering firms visit sites rather than receive clients at an office. Google says businesses that serve customers at their locations should have one profile for the central office with a designated service area. If you work from home or don't take visitors, you should hide your address. Google also says the service area generally shouldn't extend more than about two hours' drive from where you're based.

Virtual offices aren't eligible, and a co-working desk only counts if it has signage and is staffed during opening hours. If you open a second office with its own staff, it can have its own profile.

#### Choose categories carefully

Google asks for "the fewest number of categories" that describe your core business, and for categories that complete the sentence "this business IS a…". Pick the main category closest to the work you most want, then add only the secondary categories that genuinely apply.

#### Fill in everything else

Google says businesses with complete and accurate information are more likely to show in local results. Add your hours, a local phone number you control, your website, a description of your services, and photos of real projects. Site photos of steel beams, footings and finished extensions tell a homeowner more than stock images do.

### Reviews: ask every client, the right way

Reviews feed directly into prominence, and they are easy to neglect in a business where work arrives by referral. Build the request into your process. Send it when you issue the final report, certificate or calculations, while the client is still pleased you turned it around quickly.

Google's [tips to get more reviews](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122?hl=en-GB) say you can share a review link or QR code with customers. The same page is clear that offering incentives, such as discounts in exchange for reviews, counts as fake engagement and is strictly prohibited. So ask, make it easy, and leave it there.

Reply to reviews too, briefly and professionally. A calm, factual reply to a critical review shows the next reader how you deal with problems.

### What your website needs for local SEO

Your Business Profile gets you into the map results. Your website backs it up, ranks in the normal results below the map, and turns the visit into an enquiry. These are the pages that do the work.

#### Service pages for each type of work

Give each main service its own page: residential inspections, renovation and extension design, retaining walls, remedial work, subdivisions or drainage design for civil firms. Each page should say who it's for, what the client receives (a report, calculations, drawings, a certificate), typical turnaround and what you need from them to quote. A single "Services" page listing everything in bullet points doesn't give Google or the client enough to go on.

#### Service-area pages that say something real

If you cover several suburbs or towns, pages for your main areas can help. But only if each one has genuine local content: projects you've done there, the local council or building control body you deal with, common soil or housing issues in that area. Ten near-identical pages with the suburb name swapped won't help, and they make the site look thin.

#### Your registrations, shown clearly

Clients, councils and certifiers want to know who is signing off the work. In the UK, the Engineering Council says titles such as Chartered Engineer (CEng) are [protected by civil law and can only be used by people currently on its national register](https://www.engc.org.uk/professional-registration/our-professional-titles/). Registration is renewed annually through a licensed professional engineering institution.

In Victoria, Consumer Affairs Victoria explains that engineers providing professional engineering services in structural or civil engineering, among other areas, [must be registered](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/licensing-and-registration/professional-engineers/who-needs-to-be-registered). That applies in or for Victoria, so it can cover firms based interstate. Anyone can [search the public register](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/licensing-and-registration/professional-engineers/public-register) by name or registration number. If you work in other states or countries, check whether a registration scheme applies there too.

Showing your registrations, with a link to the relevant register, is a simple trust signal. Keep the details accurate and up to date, and check the current rules with your regulator or institution before deciding how to present them. This isn't legal advice.

#### A project portfolio people can actually use

Builders and architects want to see work like theirs. A filterable portfolio by sector (residential, commercial, industrial, civil) with a photo, a sentence on the problem and a sentence on what you did is more useful than a long PDF capability statement. It also gives Google real, local content to index.

#### An enquiry form that collects what you need to quote

Ask for the site address, project type, a short description and file uploads for drawings or photos. You'll spend less time chasing details, and clients see you know what you're doing. I cover this in more depth in my guide to [automating lead triage into your CRM](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html).

#### Speed and mobile

Builders and site managers often look you up on a phone, and a slow site can lose them before your number has even loaded. If you're on WordPress, my [Core Web Vitals guide](/blog/achieving-99-core-web-vitals-wordpress.html) explains what to fix.

### A local SEO checklist for structural engineers

| Area | What to check | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Business Profile name | Matches your signage and website, no added keywords | Keyword-stuffed names risk suspension |
| Address and service area | Address hidden if you don't receive visitors; service area realistic | Required by Google's guidelines |
| Categories | Fewest that describe your core work | Relevance |
| Reviews | Request sent with every final report; no incentives | Prominence, and staying within policy |
| Service pages | One page per main service, with deliverables and turnaround | Relevance, and better enquiries |
| Area pages | Only where you have genuine local content | Avoids thin, duplicate pages |
| Registrations | Shown with a link to the register, kept current | Trust for clients and certifiers |
| Portfolio | Filterable by sector, with short project notes | Proof of experience |
| Enquiry form | Address, project type, file uploads | Fewer back-and-forth emails |
| Speed | Fast on mobile | Site visitors don't leave |

### Common mistakes on engineering websites

- **Generic headlines.** "Innovative engineering solutions" doesn't tell anyone you inspect cracked walls in their suburb.
- **No location signals.** If your website never mentions the areas you cover, Google has to guess.
- **Credentials buried on the About page.** Put registrations near the enquiry form and on service pages, where people decide whether to trust you.
- **Duplicate Business Profiles.** Google's guidelines say there should be one profile per business, and that extra profiles can cause problems with how your information displays on Maps and Search. Old listings from a previous address are worth tracking down.

### How long does local SEO take?

It depends on your area and how strong the competition is. Business Profile fixes such as correct categories and a proper service area are quick to make. Reviews, links from local organisations and useful service pages build up over months. Anyone who promises a guaranteed position on the map is promising something Google says can't be bought.

### How I can help

I build and fix WordPress websites for structural and civil engineering consultancies in Australia and the UK, with the technical and local SEO set up from the start. That means service pages, service-area pages with real content, a portfolio you can filter, and enquiry forms that collect the detail you need to quote. You can see more about my [websites for structural engineers](/industries/structural-engineers/), or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like a second opinion on how your firm shows up locally, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll tell you what I'd fix first.

faq.answer: Google's guidelines say service-area businesses, meaning those that visit customers rather than receive them, should hide their address and set a service area instead. Use categories, your services and your website to show what you do and where.

faq.answer: It varies with your area and competition. Fixes to your Business Profile, such as categories and service area, are quick to make. Reviews, local links and strong service pages build up over months. Be wary of anyone promising a guaranteed map position, because Google says local ranking can't be requested or paid for.

title: How to Recruit Structural Engineers Through Your Own Website
metaTitle: How to Recruit Structural Engineers | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to recruit structural engineers through your own website: what to put on your careers page and how to get vacancies into Google's job search.
geoDirectAnswer: To recruit structural engineers through your website, build a careers page that shows the work, the people and how you support chartership or registration. Publish salary and flexibility details, give each vacancy its own page with Google's job posting structured data, remove closed roles promptly, and make applying quick on a phone.
keyTakeaways: Your careers page is the one place you control the whole story candidates hear about your firm.
Specific support for chartership, such as paid fees and mentoring, is more convincing than general promises.
Google's job posting structured data makes vacancy pages eligible for its job search, but each job needs its own page.
Closed vacancies must be expired or removed, or Google may take manual action.
In Victoria, check how registration and direct supervision apply before you describe graduate roles.
contentMarkdown:
If you're working out how to recruit structural engineers without paying an agency fee for every hire, start with your own website. Engineers often look at a firm's site before they apply, or before they agree to a recruiter's introduction. They look at the projects, the people and whether you'll support them towards chartership or registration. If your careers page is a single line saying "send your CV to info@", you're relying on agencies and job boards to do the persuading for you. This guide covers what to put on the page, how to get your vacancies into Google's job search, and the mistakes that put good candidates off.

### Why your website matters when you recruit structural engineers

Agencies and job boards are useful, but they present every firm the same way: a job title, a salary band and a location. Your website is the only place where you control the whole story. That includes the type of work, who the candidate would be working with, and how you develop people.

It also matters for Google. Google's own [job posting documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/job-posting) says that adding job posting structured data to your vacancy pages makes them eligible to appear in its job search experience. Job seekers can filter by location and job title there, so a local graduate searching "graduate structural engineer" plus your town has a way to find your firm directly.

### What a good engineering careers page includes

#### The kind of work they'll actually do

Engineers want to know whether they'll spend their days on residential extensions, commercial steel frames, remedial work, infrastructure or a mix. Say so plainly, and link to a few relevant projects in your portfolio. A short line on each project ("steel frame for a three-storey mixed-use building, designed in-house") tells a candidate more than a paragraph about "exciting opportunities".

#### Who they'll work with and learn from

Introduce the people a new starter would sit with, especially senior or chartered engineers. The Engineering Council's guidance for employers suggests [displaying employees' professional titles and post-nominal letters](https://www.engc.org.uk/professional-registration/becoming-registered/supporting-your-employees-to-become-professionally-registered/) so their achievement is recognised. On a careers page, that also shows candidates there are people around who have done it and can mentor them.

#### How you support chartership and registration

For many graduate and mid-level engineers, the path to chartership is an important factor in choosing an employer. The same Engineering Council page lists practical ways employers can support registration. These include paying membership and registration fees, sponsoring education, offering mentoring, and getting a structured graduate scheme approved or accredited against the professional standards. It notes that paying fees "is clear evidence that you place real value on the professional development of your employees".

If you do any of these things, put them on your careers page in specific terms. "We pay your institution membership and give you a mentor who is already chartered" is far more convincing than "we support professional development".

#### Registration requirements, explained honestly

In Australia, registration can affect who you can hire into which role. In Victoria, for example, Consumer Affairs Victoria explains that people providing professional engineering services in structural or civil engineering [must be registered](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/licensing-and-registration/professional-engineers/who-needs-to-be-registered). There's an exemption for work done under the direct supervision of a registered professional engineer.

That matters for graduates: tell them how supervision works at your firm and how you'll help them work towards registration. Check the current rules with the regulator in each state you work in before you write this section. This isn't legal advice.

#### Salary, hours and flexibility

Candidates compare firms side by side. If you can publish a salary range, do. If you offer hybrid working, a nine-day fortnight or study leave, say so clearly. Vague phrases like "competitive package" give people no reason to choose you over the firm whose page lists the details.

#### A simple way to apply

Ask for a CV and a short note, and make it easy to send them from a phone. Long application forms that repeat what's in the CV lose people. Tell candidates what happens next and roughly how long it takes, then stick to it.

### Getting your vacancies into Google's job search

This is the part most engineering firms miss. Google's job search experience reads structured data on your vacancy pages. According to [Google's documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/job-posting), the required properties are:

- `title`: the job title
- `description`: the full description, including responsibilities, qualifications, skills, working hours, education and experience requirements
- `datePosted`: when you posted the job
- `hiringOrganization`: your company name
- `jobLocation`: where the job is based

Recommended properties include `baseSalary`, `employmentType`, `validThrough` (the closing date) and `jobLocationType` for remote roles.

A few rules from the same page are easy to break:

- **One job per page.** Google says `JobPosting` structured data must only be on a page dedicated to a single job, not on a page that lists several vacancies. So give every role its own page, with a jobs list page linking to them.
- **Remove closed jobs promptly.** Jobs that are no longer open must be expired by setting a past `validThrough` date, removing the page, or removing the structured data. Google warns that not doing so may lead to a manual action.
- **Salary must come from you.** Google notes that only employers can provide `baseSalary`, and it should be the actual salary, not an estimate.

On WordPress this is straightforward to set up. A custom "Vacancies" post type with fields for location, salary, contract type and closing date can generate the structured data automatically. Your team then fills in a form and never touches code.

### A careers page checklist for engineering firms

| Section | What to include | Why it helps |
|---|---|---|
| Intro | Two or three lines on the work you do and where | Candidates know quickly if it's a fit |
| Projects | Three to six examples linked to your portfolio | Proof of the work, not just claims |
| People | Senior and chartered engineers with titles | Shows who they'll learn from |
| Development | Fees paid, mentoring, accredited scheme, study support | The biggest draw for graduates |
| Registration | How supervision and registration work at your firm | Answers a key question before interview |
| Pay and benefits | Salary range, hours, flexibility, leave | Lets people compare you fairly |
| Vacancies | One page per role with job posting structured data | Eligible for Google's job search |
| Applying | CV upload, short note, timeline for a reply | Fewer drop-offs |

### Before and after: a vacancy intro

Here's an invented example of a typical vacancy intro, rewritten.

**Before:** "We are looking for a talented structural engineer to join our dynamic team. Competitive salary. Send your CV to info@."

**After:** "We're hiring a graduate structural engineer for our Brisbane office. You'll work on residential extensions, small commercial buildings and remedial jobs, with a chartered engineer reviewing your designs. We pay your institution membership and give you study time towards chartership. Salary range and full details below. Apply with your CV and a short note; we reply to everyone within two weeks."

The second version answers the questions a candidate would otherwise have to ask, and it reads like a real firm rather than a template.

### Common mistakes that cost you applicants

- **Old vacancies left live.** A role that closed months ago makes the firm look disorganised, and Google's rules require closed jobs to be expired.
- **All jobs on one page.** It's tidy, but it stops each role being eligible for Google's job search.
- **No projects or people.** Without them, your careers page looks the same as every agency listing.
- **A slow, clunky site on mobile.** Candidates often browse vacancies on their phone. My [Core Web Vitals guide](/blog/achieving-99-core-web-vitals-wordpress.html) covers what to fix on WordPress.

Your careers page also benefits from the same local visibility work that brings in clients. If you haven't already, read my guide to [local SEO for structural engineers](/blog/local-seo-for-structural-engineers.html).

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for structural and civil engineering consultancies in Australia and the UK, including careers sections with a page for each vacancy and job posting structured data set up correctly. Your team adds or closes a role through a simple form. You can see more about my [websites for structural engineers](/industries/structural-engineers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like your careers page to do more of the recruiting for you, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll tell you what I'd change first.

faq.question: How do I get my engineering jobs to show on Google?
faq.answer: Give each vacancy its own page and add JobPosting structured data. Google lists title, description, datePosted, hiringOrganization and jobLocation as required properties, with salary, employment type and closing date recommended. Pages that list several jobs shouldn't carry the structured data. Remove or expire jobs once they close.

faq.question: What should a structural engineering firm put on its careers page?
faq.answer: Describe the type of work, link to real projects, introduce the senior and chartered engineers a new starter would learn from, and explain how you support chartership or registration. Add salary ranges, hours and flexibility, list each vacancy on its own page, and make it quick to apply with a CV and a short note.

faq.question: Can graduates work as structural engineers in Victoria without being registered?
faq.answer: Consumer Affairs Victoria explains that providing professional engineering services in structural engineering requires registration, but there is an exemption for work done under the direct supervision of a registered professional engineer. Check the current guidance from Consumer Affairs Victoria for how this applies to your firm and roles.

faq.question: Is it worth paying engineers' institution fees to attract staff?
faq.answer: The Engineering Council suggests paying employees' membership and registration fees as one way to support professional registration, and says the investment may be repaid through loyalty and retention. If you offer it, state it clearly on your careers page, because it answers a question many candidates have about employers.

title: Fractional CFO Website: What to Include to Win UK Clients
metaTitle: Fractional CFO Website Guide | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: What a fractional CFO website should include: service pages, pricing models, proof, booking forms and the UK legal details every firm's site must show.
geoDirectAnswer: A fractional CFO website should say clearly who you work with, which finance problems you solve, how engagements work and why you are credible. It needs service pages, a usable proof section, a booking link or short qualifying form, and for UK limited companies the required company details and a clear privacy notice.
keyTakeaways: Your homepage should answer who you help, what you solve, how it works and why you, within the first minute.
Explaining your engagement model, even without exact fees, removes a common reason prospects delay.
Case studies should be permissioned or anonymised, and if you publish reviews the CMA expects a policy prohibiting fake reviews.
UK limited companies must show their registered number, registered office and place of registration on their website.
Forms that collect personal data need clear, easily accessible privacy information at the point of collection.
contentMarkdown:
A fractional CFO website has one job: to make a founder or managing director confident enough to book a call. Most of your work probably comes through referrals and LinkedIn. But many people who hear your name will look you up before they get in touch. If your site is a single page with a stock photo of a calculator, you lose people who were already halfway to saying yes. This guide covers what a fractional CFO website should include, the UK legal basics it must get right, and how to turn visits into discovery calls. It's written for UK firms, but most of it applies anywhere.

### What a prospect wants to know in the first minute

A business owner looking at fractional CFO support usually has a specific worry. Cash is tight, they're preparing to raise money, the bank wants better forecasts, or the bookkeeping has outgrown the founder. Your homepage should answer four questions quickly:

1. **Who do you work with?** Name the stage, size or sector, for example "founder-led businesses with £2m to £20m turnover", not "businesses of all sizes".
2. **What problems do you solve?** Cash flow forecasting, fundraising readiness, board reporting, pricing, systems, exit planning.
3. **How does it work?** Days per month, retainer or project, what's included, how long a typical engagement runs.
4. **Why you?** Your background, qualifications and the kind of businesses you've helped, described accurately.

If those four answers are clear above the fold, everything else on the site is supporting detail.

### Pages every fractional CFO website should include

#### Services, written as outcomes

Give each main service its own page or section: cash flow forecasting, fundraising support, management accounts and board packs, finance function set-up, M&A or exit preparation. For each one, explain the problem, what you deliver and what the client needs to provide. "A rolling 13-week cash flow forecast, updated every fortnight, with a short call to walk through it" is more useful than "strategic cash management".

#### Who you work with

A short "ideal client" section helps the right people self-select and politely turns away the wrong ones. Sector focus, turnover range, funding stage and the kind of founder you work well with all belong here.

#### How engagements work and what they cost

Many firms hide pricing completely. You don't have to publish exact fees, but explaining the model helps a lot. Do you work on a monthly retainer, a set number of days, or fixed-price projects? Is there a minimum term? A simple "typical engagements" table removes a big reason people delay getting in touch.

#### About you, with real credentials

Owners are trusting you with their numbers. Show your professional qualifications, previous roles and sectors, and a real photo. If you hold a professional body membership, check that body's rules on how you describe yourself and your firm before you publish. Some professional titles have specific rules about how firms can use them.

#### Proof, handled carefully

Case studies are persuasive, but finance clients are often private about their numbers. Ask permission before naming a client, and consider anonymised case studies ("a SaaS business preparing for a Series A") if they'd rather not be named. Never invent results or testimonials.

If you show reviews or star ratings on your website, be aware of the UK rules. The Competition and Markets Authority's [short guide for businesses publishing consumer reviews](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fake-reviews/short-guide-for-businesses-publishing-consumer-reviews-and-complying-with-consumer-protection-law) says traders who publish reviews should have a published policy that prohibits fake reviews and sets out their approach to incentivised reviews. They must also take reasonable and proportionate steps to prevent and remove banned content. The full [CMA fake reviews guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fake-reviews) explains this in more detail. Check how it applies to your firm.

#### A contact page that books calls

The best fractional CFO websites make the next step obvious: book a 20–30 minute discovery call. Use a booking link or a short form, not just an email address. If you use a form, ask a few qualifying questions: turnover band, what prompted them to look for help, and their timeline. I explain how to route and score these enquiries automatically in my guide to [automating lead triage into your CRM](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html).

### UK legal basics your website must get right

These details are easy to overlook, and they aren't optional.

#### Company details on your website

If you trade through a limited company, GOV.UK's guidance on [signs, stationery and promotional material](https://www.gov.uk/running-a-limited-company/signs-stationery-and-promotional-material) says your website must show:

- the company's registered number
- its registered office address
- where the company is registered (England and Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland)
- the fact that it's a limited company, usually by giving the full name including "Limited" or "Ltd"

It also says that if you choose to include directors' names, you must list all of them. Most firms put these details in the website footer.

#### A proper privacy notice

Your contact form and booking tool collect personal data, so you need privacy information. The ICO's guidance on the [right to be informed](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/individual-rights/individual-rights/right-to-be-informed/) says you must give people privacy information at the time you collect their data. This includes your purposes, your lawful basis, how long you keep the data and who you share it with. It must be concise, transparent and in clear, plain language. The ICO says you can meet this by putting the information on your website, but you must make people aware of it and give them an easy way to reach it. A link next to the form's submit button is a simple way to do that.

The ICO also notes that its guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act, so check the current version. None of this is legal advice.

### Fractional CFO website checklist

| Area | What to include | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Homepage | Who you help, problems you solve, how it works, why you | Answers the first-minute questions |
| Services | One section per service, written as outcomes | Helps the right clients recognise their problem |
| Ideal client | Stage, size, sector | Filters enquiries before the call |
| Engagement model | Retainer, days or projects, minimum term | Removes a common reason to delay |
| About | Qualifications, past roles, real photo | Trust with sensitive financial work |
| Proof | Permissioned or anonymised case studies | Persuasive without breaching confidentiality |
| Reviews | Review policy if you publish reviews or ratings | CMA guidance on fake reviews |
| Contact | Booking link or short qualifying form | Turns visits into discovery calls |
| Footer | Company number, registered office, place of registration | Required for limited companies |
| Privacy | Clear privacy notice linked from forms | Right to be informed under UK GDPR |

### Getting found: SEO for fractional CFOs

Referrals will probably remain your main source of work. But a well-structured site also helps you show up when someone searches "fractional CFO" plus their city or sector, or asks an AI assistant who to talk to.

- **Write sector pages** if you specialise, such as "fractional CFO for SaaS businesses" or "fractional finance director for manufacturers". Fill them with genuine detail about that sector's finance problems.
- **Answer real questions** in articles: when a business needs a fractional CFO, how it differs from an accountant, and what a first 90 days looks like.
- **Use clear, quotable answers.** Short, direct answers near the top of a page help both Google and AI tools. My guide to [GEO and AEO](/blog/geo-aeo-generative-engine-optimization-guide.html) explains how.
- **Keep your Google Business Profile accurate** if you serve a local area. Use your real business name and the services you actually offer.

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for fractional CFO and outsourced finance firms in the UK, the US and Australia, including the Longfield Financial Advisory website in the UK. That covers clear service pages, booking and enquiry forms that qualify leads, and the footer, privacy and technical SEO details set up properly from the start. You can see more about my [websites for fractional CFO firms](/industries/fractional-cfo/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like a second opinion on your current site, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll tell you what I'd change first.

faq.answer: Explain who you work with, the finance problems you solve, how engagements work and your credentials. Add a page or section for each service, permissioned or anonymised case studies, and a booking link or short form for discovery calls. UK limited companies also need their company details on the site and a clear privacy notice.

faq.question: Should fractional CFOs publish their prices?
faq.answer: You don't have to publish exact fees, but explaining your model helps. Say whether you work on a monthly retainer, a set number of days or fixed-price projects, whether there is a minimum term, and what a typical engagement includes. That gives prospects enough to decide whether to book a call.

faq.answer: GOV.UK says a limited company's website must show its registered number, registered office address, where it is registered (England and Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland) and that it is a limited company. If you choose to include directors' names, you must list all of them. Most firms put these details in the footer.

faq.question: How do fractional CFOs get clients online?
faq.answer: Most still rely on referrals and networks, but a clear website supports them by converting people who look you up. Sector pages, articles answering real questions, a qualifying contact form and an accurate Google Business Profile can also help you appear when owners search for fractional CFO support.

title: Business Broker Website: How to Win More Seller Listings
metaTitle: Business Broker Website Guide | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to build a business broker website that wins seller listings: seller pages, valuation forms, blind listings, NDA gates and FTC testimonial rules.
geoDirectAnswer: A business broker website that wins seller listings gives owners their own path, separate from buyers. It explains the selling process, offers a valuation request, shows sector experience and fees, and proves confidentiality with blind listings and NDA-gated details. Testimonials must be genuine under the FTC rule, and private pages should use noindex.
keyTakeaways: Sellers need a separate journey from buyers, with process, valuation, fees and track record explained.
Blind listings and NDA-gated details show confidentiality in practice rather than just promising it.
Use noindex, not robots.txt, for reachable pages that shouldn't appear in Google.
Under the FTC rule, testimonials on your own site are your responsibility, and incentives tied to positive sentiment are a problem.
Your Google Business Profile name must match your real business name, without added keywords.
contentMarkdown:
Most business broker websites are built for buyers. The homepage is a grid of listings, and the "Sell your business" page is an afterthought. Yet a brokerage's growth usually depends on winning more sell-side mandates, not more buyer traffic. A business broker website that wins seller listings has to do something harder: persuade an owner who is nervous, private and often unsure whether now is the time, to have a confidential conversation with you. This guide covers the pages, forms and confidentiality features that make that happen, plus the rules on testimonials and Google listings that brokers need to get right.

### Why sellers and buyers need different journeys

Buyers arrive wanting to browse. Sellers arrive wanting reassurance. An owner thinking about selling usually wants answers to a few questions before they'll talk to anyone:

- Will this stay confidential? Will my staff, customers or competitors find out?
- What is my business likely to be worth, and how is that worked out?
- What does the process look like, how long does it take, and what will it cost me?
- Has this broker sold businesses like mine?

If your site sends sellers into the same listings grid as buyers, none of those questions get answered. Give sellers their own clear path from the homepage: a prominent "Selling your business" section with its own pages and its own call to action.

### Pages a business broker website needs for sellers

#### A "how selling works" page

Lay out your process step by step: first confidential conversation, valuation, preparing the information memorandum, marketing to buyers, screening and NDAs, offers, due diligence and closing. Say roughly how long each stage typically takes at your firm and what the owner needs to do at each step. Owners who understand the process are more likely to start it.

#### A valuation request page

A "What's my business worth?" page works well as a seller lead generator because it matches the question owners are already asking. Explain how you approach valuation in plain English. Be clear about what the owner gets: an indicative range, a written opinion of value or a formal valuation. Never promise a number before you've seen the figures.

#### Sector and deal-size pages

If you specialize, say so. Pages for the sectors you know well (healthcare practices, home services, manufacturing, e-commerce, professional services) and the deal sizes you handle help owners see themselves in your work. They also give Google specific pages to rank for searches like "sell my HVAC business" or "business broker for dental practices".

#### Fees and engagement terms, explained

You don't have to publish your fee schedule, but explain the model: success fees, any retainer or valuation fee, and the typical length of an engagement. Owners compare brokers, and silence on fees reads as a warning sign.

#### Your team and track record, described honestly

Show who will actually handle the sale, with real photos, backgrounds and any professional credentials. If you list closed deals, describe them accurately and only with the client's permission, for example "Sold: commercial cleaning business, Midwest" rather than naming a client who expected discretion.

### Confidentiality features that build trust

Confidentiality is a major worry for sellers, so your website should show it in how it works, not just say it.

#### Blind listings

Public listing pages should describe the business without identifying it: sector, broad region, revenue and cash-flow ranges, and the reason for sale, but no name, exact address or photos that give it away. Review every teaser with the seller before it goes live.

#### NDA-gated details

Put the information memorandum and identifying details behind an NDA step. A buyer requests access, signs electronically and is screened before seeing anything sensitive. This protects the seller and gives you a record of who has seen what.

#### Keep private pages out of Google

Pages that sit behind a login generally can't be crawled. But some pages may be reachable without logging in, such as "thank you" pages, NDA confirmation pages or old listings. For those, Google's documentation on [blocking indexing with noindex](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing) explains that a `noindex` meta tag or HTTP header tells Google to drop the page from its results. It also warns of a common mistake: if you block the page in robots.txt instead, Google can't see the `noindex` rule, and the page can still appear in results if other pages link to it. Most WordPress SEO plugins let you set `noindex` page by page without touching code.

### Testimonials and reviews: the FTC rule

Seller testimonials are powerful, but in the US they now come with clear rules. The FTC's [Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/consumer-reviews-testimonials-rule-questions-answers) took effect on October 21, 2024. It addresses deceptive and unfair conduct involving consumer reviews and testimonials, and courts can impose civil penalties for knowing violations.

A few points from the FTC staff's questions and answers matter for brokers:

- **Testimonials on your own site are your responsibility.** The FTC says a business that puts testimonials on its own website is disseminating them, not just "hosting" them. If those testimonials are fake or false, the business could be liable.
- **Incentives tied to sentiment are a problem.** The rule covers compensation or incentives conditioned on reviews expressing a particular sentiment. Asking every client for honest feedback is fine; rewarding only positive reviews is not.
- **Insiders need care.** The rule includes disclosure requirements for certain situations involving company insiders, so staff or partners shouldn't post reviews of your firm without making the relationship clear.

The FTC notes its staff guidance isn't definitive, so check the current guidance and take legal advice if you're unsure. This isn't legal advice.

### Local SEO for business brokers

Many owners search locally: "business broker near me" or "business broker" plus their city. Your Google Business Profile matters here. Google's [guidelines for representing your business](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177?hl=en-GB) say your profile name should match your real-world business name, and that adding extra keywords or service information to it isn't permitted and could get the profile suspended. If you meet clients at your office, show the address. If you don't receive visitors, set a service area and hide the address instead.

On your own site, back this up with a page for each main area you serve, with genuine local content: the types of businesses you've sold there and the local market you know.

### Business broker website checklist

| Area | What to include | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Homepage | Separate, prominent paths for sellers and buyers | Sellers don't get lost in listings |
| Selling process | Step-by-step stages and rough timings | Reduces fear of the unknown |
| Valuation page | Plain-English approach and a short request form | Matches the question owners ask first |
| Sector pages | Sectors and deal sizes you handle | Owners see themselves; better rankings |
| Fees | Your fee model and engagement terms | Silence on fees puts people off |
| Track record | Permissioned, anonymized closed deals | Proof without breaching confidentiality |
| Listings | Blind teasers with NDA-gated details | Protects sellers and screens buyers |
| Private pages | `noindex` on pages that shouldn't be in Google | Keeps sensitive pages out of results |
| Testimonials | Genuine, unincentivized, with insider relationships disclosed | FTC rule compliance |
| Local SEO | Accurate Business Profile and real area pages | Shows up for "business broker near me" |

### Turning visits into seller conversations

A seller inquiry form should be short and reassuring. Ask for their name, a contact method, the type of business, an approximate revenue band and a rough timeline. State clearly that the inquiry is confidential and who will see it. Offer a phone number and a booking link too, because many owners prefer to talk first.

Then follow up quickly. Routing seller and buyer inquiries to the right person automatically, and scoring them by deal size and timeline, saves hours. I explain how in my guide to [automating lead triage into your CRM](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html). For showing up in AI search tools, see my guide to [GEO and AEO](/blog/geo-aeo-generative-engine-optimization-guide.html).

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for business brokers and business acquisition firms in the US and the UK. That covers separate seller and buyer journeys, valuation and inquiry forms, blind listings with NDA-gated details, and the technical and local SEO set up correctly. You can see more about my [websites for business brokers](/industries/business-brokers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like more seller mandates from your website, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll tell you what I'd change first.

faq.question: How do business brokers get more listings?
faq.answer: Referrals from accountants, attorneys and past clients remain important, but your website should also convert owners who look you up. Give sellers their own section explaining the process, a valuation request page, sector pages, your fee model and anonymized closed deals, with a short confidential inquiry form and a phone number.

faq.question: What should a business broker website include?
faq.answer: Separate paths for sellers and buyers, a step-by-step selling process, a valuation request page, sector and deal-size pages, an explanation of fees, your team and permissioned track record, blind listings with NDA-gated details, and an accurate Google Business Profile backed by genuine local area pages.

faq.question: How do brokers keep business listings confidential online?
faq.answer: Publish blind teasers that describe the sector, broad region and financial ranges without identifying the business. Put the information memorandum and identifying details behind an NDA step with buyer screening. For any reachable page that shouldn't appear in Google, use a noindex tag rather than blocking it in robots.txt.

faq.question: Can business brokers use client testimonials on their website?
faq.answer: Yes, if they're genuine. The FTC says a business that puts testimonials on its own website is disseminating them and could be liable if they're fake or false. Don't offer incentives conditioned on positive sentiment, and make insider relationships clear. Check the FTC's current guidance and get legal advice if unsure.
